text:
“How am I to understand it!” her father cried angrily. “Prince Vasili finds you to his taste as a daughter-in-law and makes you a proposal on behalf of his ward. That is how you are to understand it. ‘How am I to understand it?!’... And I am asking you.”

“I do not know what you think, Father,” the princess said in a whisper.

“I? I? What have I to do with it? Leave me out of it. I am not the one who is going to marry. What do you think? That is what I should like to know.”

The princess saw that her father regarded the matter unfavorably, but at that very moment the thought came to her that now or never the fate of her life would be decided. She lowered her eyes so as not to see the gaze under whose influence she felt that she could not think, but could only obey out of habit, and said:

“I desire only one thing—to carry out your will,” she said, “but if my own desire had to be expressed...”

She did not have time to finish. The prince interrupted her.

“And splendid!” he shouted. “He will take you with your dowry, and pick up Mlle Bourienne into the bargain. She will be the wife, and you...”

The prince stopped. He noticed the effect these words had produced on his daughter. She lowered her head and was about to cry.

“Come, come, I am joking, I am joking,” he said. “Remember one thing, Princess: I adhere to the rule that a maiden has a perfect right to choose. And I give you freedom. Remember one thing: the happiness of your life depends on your decision. There is no need to speak of me.”

“But I do not know... Father.”

“There is no need to speak! He is ordered to; he will marry not only you, but anyone they please; while you are free to choose... Go to your room, think it over, and in an hour come to me and say in his presence: yes or no.

“I know you will pray. Well, pray if you like. Only it would be better to think. Go.”

“Yes or no, yes or no, yes or no!” he was still shouting as the princess, as though in a fog, already staggered out of the study.

Her fate was decided, and decided happily. But what her father had said about Mlle Bourienne—that insinuation was terrible. Granted, it was not true, but still it was terrible; she could not help thinking about it. She was walking straight ahead through the conservatory, seeing and hearing nothing, when suddenly Mlle Bourienne’s familiar whisper roused her. She raised her eyes and, two paces away, saw Anatole embracing the Frenchwoman and whispering something to her. With a terrible expression on his handsome face, Anatole looked round at Princess Marya and, during the first instant, did not release the waist of Mlle Bourienne, who had not seen her.

“Who is there? Why? Wait!” Anatole’s face seemed to say. Princess Marya looked at them in silence. She could not understand it. At last Mlle Bourienne gave a cry and ran away. With a cheerful smile, Anatole bowed to Princess Marya, as though inviting her to laugh at this strange incident, and, shrugging his shoulders, went through the door leading to his quarters.

An hour later Tikhon came to summon Princess Marya. He summoned her to the prince and added that Prince Vasili Sergeyevich was there as well. When Tikhon came, the princess was sitting on the sofa in her room, holding the weeping Mlle Bourienne in her arms. Princess Marya was gently stroking her head. The princess’s beautiful eyes, with all their former serenity and radiance, looked with tender love and pity at Mlle Bourienne’s pretty little face.

“No, Princess, I am lost forever in your heart,” said Mlle Bourienne.

“Why? I love you more than ever,” said Princess Marya, “and I shall try to do everything in my power for your happiness.”

“But you despise me; you, who are so pure, will never understand this aberration of passion. Ah, it is only my poor mother...”

“I understand everything,” Princess Marya replied with a sad smile. “Calm yourself, my friend. I shall go to my father,” she said, and went out.

Prince Vasili, with one leg crossed high and a snuffbox in his hands, looking as though he were moved beyond measure, as though he himself both pitied and laughed at his own sensitivity, was sitting with a smile of tender emotion on his face when Princess Marya entered. He hastily raised a pinch of snuff to his nose.

“Ah, my dear, my dear,” he said, rising and taking her by both hands. He sighed and added, “My son’s fate is in your hands. Decide, my dear, my darling, my sweet Marie, whom I have always loved as my own daughter.”

He stepped away. A genuine tear appeared in his eyes.

“Frr... frr...” Prince Nikolai Andreyevich snorted.

“The prince, on behalf of his ward... his son, is making you a proposal. Do you or do you not wish to be the wife of Prince Anatole Kuragin? You say yes or no!” he shouted. “And afterward I reserve the right to state my own opinion as well. Yes, my opinion, and only my own opinion,” Prince Nikolai Andreyevich added, turning to Prince Vasili and responding to his imploring expression. “Yes or no?”

“My desire, Father, is never to leave you, never to separate my life from yours. I do not wish to marry,” she said resolutely, looking with her beautiful eyes at Prince Vasili and at her father.

“Nonsense, foolishness! Nonsense, nonsense, nonsense!” Prince Nikolai Andreyevich shouted with a frown. He took his daughter by the hand, bent her toward him, and did not kiss her, but merely bent his forehead to hers and touched her; and he squeezed the hand he was holding so hard that she winced and cried out.

Prince Vasili rose.

“My dear, I shall tell you that this is a moment I shall never, never forget; but, my dear, will you not give us a little hope of moving this heart, so kind, so generous? Say that perhaps... The future is so vast. Say: perhaps.”

“Prince, what I have said is all that is in my heart. I thank you for the honor, but I shall never be your son’s wife.”

“Well, that is settled, my dear fellow. Very glad to see you, very glad to see you. Go to your room, Princess, go,” said the old prince. “Very, very glad to see you,” he repeated, embracing Prince Vasili.

“My calling is a different one,” Princess Marya thought to herself. “My calling is to be happy with another kind of happiness, the happiness of love and self-sacrifice. And whatever it may cost me, I shall make poor Amélie happy. She loves him so passionately. She repents so passionately. I shall do everything to arrange her marriage to him. If he is not rich, I shall give her the means; I shall ask Father, I shall ask Andrei. I shall be so happy when she is his wife. She is so unhappy, a stranger, alone, without help! And, my God, how passionately she loves him, if she could so forget herself. Perhaps I would have done the same!...” thought Princess Marya.
